claims.text: Social media use is significantly and positively associated with appearance anxiety among university students.
Upward social comparison mediates the relationship between social media use and appearance anxiety.
Envy mediates the relationship between social media use and appearance anxiety.
Upward social comparison and envy form a significant chain mediating pathway between social media use and appearance anxiety.
The direct effect of social media use on appearance anxiety remains significant after accounting for upward social comparison and envy.

evidence.description: The total effect of social media use on appearance anxiety was significant (B = 0.5700, SE = 0.0196, 95% CI [0.5315, 0.6085], p < 0.001) with a bivariate correlation of r = 0.642 (p < 0.001).

Bootstrap analysis demonstrated a significant indirect effect for Social media use -> upward social comparison -> appearance anxiety (effect = 0.2182, BootSE = 0.0232, 95% bootstrap CI [0.1736, 0.2644]).
Bootstrap analysis demonstrated a significant indirect effect for Social media use -> envy -> appearance anxiety (effect = 0.1069, BootSE = 0.0146, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0796, 0.1362]).

Bootstrap analysis showed a significant chain indirect effect for Social media use -> upward social comparison -> envy -> appearance anxiety (effect = 0.1043, BootSE = 0.0129, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0798, 0.1303]), with total indirect effect accounting for 75.333% of the total effect.

After controlling for mediators and covariates, the direct association between social media use and appearance anxiety remained significant (B = 0.1406, SE = 0.0225, 95% CI [0.0964, 0.1848], p < 0.001).

methodologies.name: Chain mediation analysis with Hayes PROCESS Model 6
methodologies.description: A cross-sectional survey evaluating chain mediation via multiple regression and 5,000 percentile bootstrap samples controlling for gender, educational level, and daily social media use time.
datasets: Self-report survey of 1,640 Chinese university students across >20 institutions
conditions: Controlled for gender, educational level, and average daily social media use time
5,000 percentile bootstrap resamples for indirect effect confidence intervals

limitations.text: The study used a cross-sectional design where all variables were measured at a single time point, precluding causal inference or establishment of temporal order.
All core variables relied on self-report instruments from the same participants, which may introduce social desirability, recall bias, and common method variance.
Social media use was assessed as a global construct without distinguishing active posting from passive browsing, platform types, or appearance-focused features like filter use and selfie editing.
Participant age was not collected or controlled for, and convenience sampling across a non-representative distribution of institutions limits generalizability.
The model did not test boundary conditions or potential moderators such as gender, body appreciation, self-esteem, media literacy, or self-compassion.

Prior research insufficiently differentiated between sociocultural sources of appearance pressure and psychological responses, and frequently relied on single mediators or non-appearance-specific distress outcomes.

future_work.text: Use multiwave longitudinal designs, cross-lagged panel models, or randomized experiments to determine causal directionality and temporal sequencing of the comparison-envy-anxiety pathway.
Incorporate objective usage records, platform behavior logs, experience sampling, and interviews to mitigate self-report biases.
Differentiate platform types, content categories, and specific behaviors such as algorithmic recommendations, filter usage, and selfie editing.
Utilize stratified random sampling and multigroup analyses to identify boundary conditions and demographic subgroups most susceptible to upward comparison and envy.
